name: The Handkerchief Tree of Assistens

location.address: Assistens Kirkegård, Section A, near the northeast corner (Nørrebrogade / Kapelvej), Nørrebro, Copenhagen

access: Free, open access; Assistens Kirkegård functions as both cemetery and public park, open 07:00-22:00 in summer and 07:00-19:00 in winter
transport: Nørrebros Runddel metro station (M3 Cityringen), roughly 5-7 minute walk; the station sits at the cemetery's northeastern corner, close to this tree
verify_notes: Two independent sources: the Danish Dendrological Society's own register (surveyed by Hans Erik Lund, 26-11-2019, GPS-verified, status 'levende, sund' / alive and healthy, two-to-multi-stemmed, circumference 1.4m, diameter 0.45m) and bennyfriisgunno.dk, an independent Danish nature-photography site describing the same tree by name and location ('near the Monkey Puzzle Tree, section A'). Species is Davidia involucrata, called duetræ (dove tree) in Danish and handkerchief/pocket-handkerchief tree in English; the large white bracts that surround the flower head in May look like doves or handkerchiefs hanging in the crown. Native to China, first brought into Western cultivation by Ernest Wilson in 1904; still uncommon in Danish gardens. No planting date found for this specimen anywhere; age_estimate is honestly 'not documented'. The age range given (40-100) is a rough inference only, from the tree's modest circumference at the 2019 survey and the species' rarity in Denmark before the mid-20th century, not a measured or sourced figure, so it should read as a wide guess in the story, not a fact. Multi-stemmed growth form, worth noting for the writer. GPS from the dendrological register is tree-level and verified in the field (not park-level), hence 'confirmed' precision. Assistens Kirkegård itself is a well-known public cemetery-park in Nørrebro, founded 1757/1760, free and open daily; graves of H.C. Andersen and Kierkegaard are nearby, useful walk context.

name: The Weeping Beech of Assistens

location.address: Assistens Kirkegård, Section B, just right of the entrance from Kapelvej, Nørrebro, Copenhagen

access: Free, open access; Assistens Kirkegård functions as both cemetery and public park, open 07:00-22:00 in summer and 07:00-19:00 in winter
transport: Nørrebros Runddel metro station (M3 Cityringen) or the Kapelvej main entrance, roughly 5-10 minute walk
verify_notes: Two independent sources: the Danish Dendrological Society's register (surveyed by Hans Erik Lund, 26-11-2019, GPS-verified, circumference 3.29m, height 15m, diameter 1.05m, status 'levende'/alive, single-stemmed) and bennyfriisgunno.dk, an independent site that separately describes a weeping beech in the same part of the cemetery ('section B, opposite the wall to the local cemetery') as the largest specimen there. The register notes the graft union is clearly visible at about 1m height with the grafted scion growing faster than the rootstock (not unusual for the cultivar), and flags 'a large wound at the base of the trunk / near the root', so vitality carries a caveat worth stating honestly rather than dropping. No planting date found; age_estimate is 'not documented'. The 80-150 year range is a rough inference from the 3.29m circumference against typical Fagus sylvatica growth rates, not a sourced or measured figure, and reads as a wide guess for the story rather than fact. Weeping beeches (sørgebøg) are a common 19th/20th-century cemetery ornamental in Denmark, so a planting sometime after the cemetery's romantic-era plantings (roughly mid-1800s onward) is plausible but unconfirmed.

name: The Great Maple of Assistens

location.address: Assistens Kirkegård, Section C, roughly 10m southwest of the section's centre, Nørrebro, Copenhagen

access: Free, open access; Assistens Kirkegård functions as both cemetery and public park, open 07:00-22:00 in summer and 07:00-19:00 in winter
transport: Nørrebros Runddel metro station (M3 Cityringen), roughly 10 minute walk
verify_notes: Two independent sources, though the second is thinner than usual: the Danish Dendrological Society's register (Hans Erik Lund, 26-11-2019, GPS-verified, circumference 4.19m, height 22.5m, diameter 1.33m, status 'levende, sund'/alive and healthy, single-stemmed but forking into two from about 2m up, 'regionalt bemaerkelsesvaerdig'/regionally noteworthy, the largest-girth tree registered at Assistens) and bennyfriisgunno.dk, an independent site that lists maple (loenn) among the cemetery's notable trees worth seeing, with a photograph, though without the register's level of individual detail, so treat the second source as confirming the species is a known feature of the cemetery rather than pinpointing this exact specimen. No planting date found anywhere; age_estimate is 'not documented'. The 100-180 year range is a rough inference from the 4.19m circumference (the largest of any tree registered at Assistens) against typical Acer pseudoplatanus growth, not a sourced or measured figure. Sycamore maple is an ordinary, hardy species rather than an exotic one, so its case for inclusion rests on being the single largest tree in the cluster and clearing the 'genuinely old' bar on girth alone, worth the writer weighing against the more exotic cop_006/cop_007 entries.

name: The Beech by the Boat Trip

location.address: Frederiksberg Have, beside the Bådfarten (rowing-boat rental/canal boat trip), Frederiksberg

access: Free, open access; Frederiksberg Have is a public park, protected (fredet) under Danish nature conservation law
transport: Frederiksberg Allé metro station (M1/M2/M3), roughly 10-12 minute walk via Frederiksberg Runddel, the garden's main entrance
verify_notes: Two sources, of different kinds rather than two specimen-level accounts: the Danish Dendrological Society's register (Hans Erik Lund, 12-10-2016, GPS-verified, circumference 4.68m, diameter 1.49m, status 'levende'/alive, single-stemmed, given the alternate name 'Bogen ved badfarten', the beech by the boat trip, tying it to a known landmark) and the Danish heritage agency's own published guide to Frederiksberg Have (fredninger.dk PDF), which confirms beech (bog) as one of the garden's characteristic species and documents the garden generally as a protected Romantic landscape garden (redesigned 1798-1804 from an earlier Baroque layout) with trees that include some planted 300+ years ago (the heritage source names the Mathildehoje lindens specifically for that superlative, not this beech, so the 300-year figure is NOT claimed for this tree). No planting date exists for this specific beech; age_estimate is honestly 'not documented'. The 120-220 year range is a rough inference from its 4.68m circumference, one of the largest recorded in this project's Copenhagen work so far, against typical European beech growth, not a sourced or measured figure. Named for the garden's rowing-boat trips (badfarten), a still-operating visitor feature, which gives the story a concrete, findable landmark to anchor on beyond GPS coordinates alone.

name: The Pedunculate Oak of Frederiksberg Have
access: Free, open access; Frederiksberg Have is a public park, protected (fredet) under Danish nature conservation law
transport: Frederiksberg Alle metro station (M1/M2/M3), roughly 10-15 minute walk via Frederiksberg Runddel, the garden's main entrance
verify_notes: Two sources, again of different kinds: the Danish Dendrological Society's register (Hans Erik Lund, 12-10-2016, GPS-verified, circumference 4.95m, height 28.8m, diameter 1.58m, status 'levende'/alive, single-stemmed, rated 'kommunalt bemaerkelsesvaerdig'/municipally noteworthy, the largest-girth tree found in either Copenhagen cluster this pass) and the Danish heritage agency's published guide to Frederiksberg Have (fredninger.dk PDF), which lists 'stilk-eg' (pedunculate oak) among the garden's characteristic old species and documents the garden's status as a protected Romantic landscape garden with trees dating back centuries in places (the 300+ year superlative is given there for the Mathildehoje lindens specifically, not claimed here for this oak). No planting date found for this individual tree; age_estimate is 'not documented'. The 130-250 year range is a rough inference from its 4.95m circumference, the single largest girth measured in this pass, against typical Quercus robur growth rates for parkland trees, not a sourced or measured figure, and should read as a wide guess for the story. The garden itself was redesigned into its current Romantic, landscape form in 1798-1804 from an earlier Baroque layout (originally laid out around 1700), which sets a plausible outer bound: this oak cannot predate the garden's founding as royal grounds.
